title: Hardware-Software Co-Design In The AI Era
gist: Integrated hardware/software co-design remains blocked less by technology than by structure: separate teams, tools, languages and cadences, plus the absence of hardware models fast and accurate enough to run full workloads before silicon. EDA vendors (Synopsys, Siemens EDA) and IP players (MIPS/GlobalFoundries, RISC-V International, Normal Computing, Quadric) are pushing spec-driven flows, cloud FPGA continuous integration and ontology-based virtual prototypes, but AI today is confined to RTL and testbench generation, not architectural trade-offs — and the author concludes the decades-old status quo is unlikely to change.

themes.theme: Structural split between hardware and software teams

insights.claim: In most chip companies the software team only picks up the design after silicon ships, absorbing every late change and every erratum, which leaves them saturated and unable to participate in designing the next-generation chip.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Co-design promises from chip vendors are org-chart claims first; check whether software leads sit in architecture reviews before believing time-to-market guidance.
insights.quote: The reality is the chip gets out, then the software team picks it up. They have to deal with everything that’s changed, every piece of errata.
insights.locator: Team structure — "If you look at decoupled hardware-software teams"

insights.claim: Only a couple of architects and microarchitectural designers at a typical company actually understand the hardware/software interface, so collaboration cannot scale until hardware-side tools are brought into the software developers' existing environment.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The addressable market for co-design tooling is the 'army of software developers,' not the handful of architects EDA sells to today — a potential seat-count expansion for whoever cracks it.
insights.quote: That’s what we call software-driven hardware design.
insights.locator: Team structure — "How do you bring the tools used by the hardware team into the software world?"

insights.claim: Companies that can understand a workload, build and customize the chip for it, and reach market fast will lead, reversing the old sequence of building a chip first and enabling the ecosystem afterwards.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Favors vertically integrated workload owners (hyperscaler silicon teams) over merchant chip vendors that ship hardware and hope software follows.
insights.quote: That is a significant paradigm shift that will impact the entire semiconductor industry.
insights.locator: Team structure — "The people most likely to become leaders"

insights.claim: Hardware and software development cadences differ, the cost of an error is asymmetric between the two domains, and the tools and languages are inconsistent, which is why decades of co-design advocacy never produced an integrated flow.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Structural incentives, not missing tools, are the binding constraint — discount EDA roadmaps that assume tooling alone fixes it.
insights.locator: Conclusion — "The industry has long wanted to bring hardware and software development closer together"

themes.theme: Latency of iteration as the core metric

insights.claim: The controlling variable in hardware/software integration is latency — the time to reach a conclusion — and waiting for silicon makes that latency equal to the entire project timeline.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions, Synopsys
insights.so_what: A clean way to value EDA products: price them against the iteration latency they remove, not feature lists.
insights.quote: If you wait until you have silicon, the latency is the project timeline.
insights.locator: Team structure — "The overarching challenge is latency"

insights.claim: Specification engineering — deriving RTL, models and software from a single spec — could make design iteration lightning fast, shifting the bottleneck from design creation to simulation speed.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions, Synopsys
insights.so_what: If specs become the compilable source of truth, simulation/emulation capacity becomes the scarce resource and the pricing power moves there.
insights.quote: The iteration could be lightning fast. Now it’s becoming a question: ‘Can you simulate it fast enough?'
insights.locator: Team structure — "The good news is the rapid development toward specification engineering"

insights.claim: AWS ports RISC-V IP to FPGAs and makes them available in the cloud, so modifying a line of Verilog can regenerate FPGA images and push them to cloud instances, giving hardware the same continuous-integration loop software already has.
insights.speaker: Andrea Gallo, CEO, RISC-V International
insights.so_what: Cloud FPGA CI is a concrete on-ramp for hyperscalers to compress silicon design cycles — watch AWS FPGA instance usage and RISC-V ecosystem tooling.
insights.quote: As soon as you modify a line of Verilog it will generate FPGA images and upload them into the cloud.
insights.locator: Team structure — "AWS explained its process"

insights.claim: A spec-derived ontology can serve as the source of truth for software development, letting software be written against the ontology before any RTL exists.
insights.speaker: Yaron Ilani, design verification solutions engineer, Normal Computing
insights.so_what: A startup wedge: if ontologies replace RTL as the handoff artifact, the incumbents' RTL-centric tool chains lose their gatekeeper position.
insights.quote: We can develop software against the ontology, which is a source of truth derived from the spec.
insights.locator: Team structure — "This is enabled by virtual prototyping"

insights.claim: Customers have moved past synthetic workloads and now demand that virtual prototypes run the full software stack and true system-level workloads, forcing continuity between model types that historically did not connect.
insights.speaker: Andy Meier, principal product marketing manager, Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Demand is shifting toward full-stack pre-silicon validation — a revenue tailwind for vendors with connected virtual-platform-to-emulation-to-prototype flows.
insights.quote: They are not using them for synthetic workloads, or a small subset of the system. They want to run the full stack, or true system-level workloads.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "Today, we are seeing software defining the solution"

insights.claim: Wall-clock time, not just accuracy, is the practical limit on pre-silicon workload execution: ten seconds of silicon time is realistically unattainable in simulation or emulation, so teams must decide what fraction to cover.
insights.speaker: Andy Meier, principal product marketing manager, Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Sets a hard ceiling on pre-silicon coverage claims and explains the structural demand for ever-larger emulation capacity.
insights.quote: If they need 10 seconds of silicon time, is that realistic in simulation or emulation? Probably not.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "This presents a challenge beyond performance and accuracy trade-offs"

insights.claim: Emulation capacity is a major industry topic because full-chip workload runs require modular verification — replicating individual subsystems and connecting them within or across multiple emulators.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions, Synopsys
insights.so_what: Emulator capacity expansion is a recurring hardware capex line for EDA vendors and a leading indicator of large SoC program starts.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "There are several axes here"

insights.claim: Each verification platform has a distinct sweet spot — virtual prototypes show software impact on architecture but cannot analyze coherency issues, emulation delivers performance and power analysis, FPGA prototyping delivers real-time interfaces — and teams need all of them at different cost points.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions, Synopsys
insights.so_what: No single platform wins; vendors selling only one point on the continuum are structurally disadvantaged versus full-portfolio suppliers.
insights.quote: People need everything, each with a different latency.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "It may start with a virtual prototype"

insights.claim: The deliverable of a design flow should shift from RTL or netlist handoffs to the simulated platform itself, creating a continuum from design through application support to end-customer support.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: If the simulated platform becomes the product artifact, IP vendors gain a recurring-support surface beyond one-time RTL licensing.
insights.quote: we’re no longer talking about handing off RTL or a netlist. Those are just pieces that pop out of a design flow.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "Something is missing"

insights.claim: Keeping a high-level untimed SystemC virtual platform in sync with RTL consumes large amounts of engineering time, and industry data shows verification, validation and software bring-up are where time is spent — making it the area most ripe for improvement.
insights.speaker: Andy Meier, principal product marketing manager, Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Verification and bring-up are the largest cost pools in chip development — the highest-leverage target for any AI-for-EDA investment thesis.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "You have to recognize that there is a difference"

insights.claim: Engineers do not need every system detail and instead rely on heuristics — whether the system is functional end to end, whether the power profile of a sequence is understood, whether pipeline behavior is understood — assembled from a collection of simulation technologies that never run together.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Explains why a single unified model never emerges; the value sits in stitching partial datasets, a workflow/data problem more than a simulator problem.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "There’s a lot of heuristics"

themes.theme: Where AI actually helps — and where it does not

insights.claim: Customers are applying AI almost exclusively to RTL creation and testbench creation, with no visible adoption in architecture, because architectural trade-offs still depend on deep human knowledge.
insights.speaker: Andy Meier, principal product marketing manager, Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: AI-in-EDA revenue today is concentrated in code and testbench generation; claims of AI-driven architecture exploration are still forward-looking.
insights.quote: They are primarily utilizing it for RTL creation and test bench creation. I’m not seeing it in architecture.
insights.locator: Team structure — "We are watching how our customers are utilizing AI"

insights.claim: System-level constraints such as cost, form factor, power budget, thermal limits and environmental factors have never been encoded in a form an AI algorithm could use as an optimization goal, which is why AI cannot yet take on architectural co-design.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Encoding system constraints as machine-readable objectives is the unlock; any vendor claiming AI architecture exploration without it is overselling.
insights.locator: Intro — "But there are constraints to consider when making these decisions"

insights.claim: Because almost no co-design examples exist to train on, AI may have to generate its own data by running synthetic experiments measuring how software functions perform in timing and power across an array of hardware architectures before it can make informed co-design decisions.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Training-data scarcity, not model capability, gates AI co-design — whoever owns proprietary architecture/workload measurement data holds the moat.
insights.locator: Intro — "With the promise of AI helping in both hardware and software domains"

insights.claim: Chip IP companies are already using AI agents to write hardware as well as software, but deploy them in targeted ways because the models' limitations and faults must be understood.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Confirms agentic RTL generation is in production use at IP vendors, though scoped — an early productivity signal rather than headcount displacement.
insights.quote: You cannot just take it as this perfect model that’s going to solve all the world’s problems.
insights.locator: Help from AI — "We and other companies are using AI"

insights.claim: AI shows early ability to manage cross-abstraction-layer dependencies better than individual developers, and tighter coupling from product surface and software down to firmware and hardware is the gating factor for hardware and software that recursively improve each other.
insights.speaker: Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer, Normal Computing
insights.so_what: The 'recursive self-improvement of hardware+software' north star is the long-duration bull case for AI-native EDA startups.
insights.quote: And that’s a gating factor to an even more ambitious north star – software and hardware that recursively improves.
insights.locator: Help from AI — "AI has shown some nascent ability"

insights.claim: Because LLMs let both programmers and AI assistants rewrite and expand software countless times, the algorithm set assumed in the co-design virtual model at project start no longer matches the software running two years later when silicon is ready.
insights.speaker: Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer, Quadric
insights.so_what: Argues for programmable/flexible accelerators over workload-frozen fixed-function silicon — a direct pitch against narrowly optimized ASICs.
insights.quote: two years later when silicon is ready, the software itself has been rewritten and improved/expanded countless times by both programmers and AI assistants.
insights.locator: Help from AI — "A big impact of AI for software is the ability of AI models"

insights.claim: Co-design can only be treated as a single point in time rather than a continuous process, because software iterates far faster than the silicon it targets.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Any ROI model for co-design tooling must discount for workload drift over the multi-year silicon cycle.
insights.locator: Help from AI — "Software iterations make it difficult to treat co-design"

insights.claim: UVM was designed so humans could reuse verification components in a standardized structure, and that human-readability rationale may now be obsolete — agentic flows may not need methodologies whose sole purpose is human maintainability.
insights.speaker: Yaron Ilani, design verification solutions engineer, Normal Computing
insights.so_what: If agentic verification displaces UVM, decades of tool and training investment in UVM-centric EDA lose defensive value.
insights.quote: Maybe we don’t need the extra complexity of methodologies whose sole purpose is to be human-readable or human-maintainable.
insights.locator: Help from AI — "Take verification, for example"

insights.claim: EDA users optimize individual waterfall steps for local productivity rather than jointly optimizing for global outcomes, and closing that gap requires systems of record that track how design collateral links together plus verification loops factored against that record.
insights.speaker: Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer, Normal Computing
insights.so_what: A 'system of record for chip design collateral' is named as a hard but high-value unsolved problem — a startup category to watch.
insights.quote: People aren’t jointly optimizing for global outcomes.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "A lot of that is unsolved within the EDA space"

insights.claim: AI black boxes in chip design still require guarantees of correctness and auditability, which is why adoption arrives as incremental improvement to existing methodologies rather than wholesale replacement — risk minimization dominates.
insights.speaker: Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer, Normal Computing
insights.so_what: Expect slow, incremental AI-EDA revenue ramps rather than step-function disruption; incumbents' installed base is protected by audit requirements.
insights.locator: Gaps remain — "Most advances come from incremental improvement"

insights.claim: Building specifications rich and complete enough to be consumed by both humans and AI agents is the first prerequisite for co-design, and outside of military/aerospace almost no industry does this today.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Defense/aerospace suppliers hold an unusual structural advantage in spec-driven AI design flows; everyone else must build the spec discipline first.
insights.quote: Outside of Mil/Aero, few industries do this today.
insights.locator: Intro — "The first challenge is constructing specifications"

insights.claim: The most performant design workflow is entirely bespoke to the task at hand, and the permanent trade-off is between how general-purpose a workflow is and how performant it is.
insights.speaker: Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer, Normal Computing
insights.so_what: Explains why horizontal AI design tools underperform vertical ones — bet on task-specific tooling in the near term.
insights.quote: The trade-off has always been between how flexible or general-purpose a workflow is, and how performant it is,
insights.locator: Intro — "says Arvind Srinivasan, design verification solutions engineer at Normal Computing"

insights.claim: For most of the semiconductor industry's life, hardware was the high-value element onto which software was ported; today software defines almost everything and hardware's role is merely to execute it as fast as possible.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Frames the value-capture inversion: pricing power migrates to whoever defines the workload, not whoever fabricates the part.
insights.locator: Conclusion — "For most of the life of the semiconductor industry"

insights.claim: Close hardware/software collaboration is not actually required beyond a few experts from each team, so despite the AI wave the industry is likely to stay exactly where it has always been.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A direct fade on co-design hype: be skeptical of EDA and IP vendor narratives that price in a structural co-design transition.
insights.quote: That is where we have always been, and it doesn’t really appear as if the future will be different.
insights.locator: Conclusion — "None of this requires particularly close collaboration"
